CorrFlow: Self-Correcting Flow Matching

Hangwei Zhang Affiliation: PVG, Nanyang Technological University    Nathan Rouillé Affiliation: PVG, Nanyang Technological University Affiliation: Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris    Chuanxia Zheng Affiliation: PVG, Nanyang Technological University
Abstract

Flow-matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model’s clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base-model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theory gives conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw-input affine predictors, refiner training outperforms continued base-model training at matched compute, and deployed correction lowers velocity error under its own sampler law. Experiments on class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow-project.

1 Introduction

Flow-matching models (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) generate samples by learning a velocity field that transports noise toward the data distribution. Their simple regression objective has shown strong results in image (Esser et al., 2024), video (Wan et al., 2025), 3D (Xiang et al., 2025) and robotic action (Black et al., 2024). Yet generated content still exhibits structural errors, semantic mismatches and physical inconsistencies (Zheng et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Motamed et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a). Recent approaches improve generation quality through large-scale training (Esser et al., 2024), representation alignment (Yu et al., 2025), self-supervised feature learning (Chefer et al., 2026) and reward-based optimization (Yuan et al., 2026). They focus on improving the model’s ability by learning only from the final answer, which is limited. This limitation can be attributed, in part, to the fact that the model must predict a single velocity to determine the next sample state, without any opportunity to review and revise its own predictions.

We therefore exploit the property that learning should be “refine-in-loop”, in the sense that if a student makes a mistake, e.g., in an examination, they should revisit the answer they wrote, the question they were asked, and the reasoning they followed. By examining these pieces of context together, the student can trace a mistake and determine how to revise it, rather than struggling with a final answer (Madaan et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025). Inspired by the success of self-refinement in large language models (LLMs) (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), we apply this principle to flow matching. A flow-based generator already computes analogous information at each sampling step: an estimate of the clean sample→\rightarrowanswer, the generation conditions→\rightarrowquestion and intermediate hidden states→\rightarrowinternal state. The challenge is to define a correction target that can be supervised during training and predicted from these quantities without access to a clean reference during generation.

In this paper, we introduce CorrFlow , a self-correcting flow-matching framework that attaches a lightweight refiner to the base generator. Our core insight is that the model’s one-step clean prediction provides a concrete object for the review, with a direct mathematical connection to the correction we seek (Chen et al., 2022). Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error between this prediction and the clean sample is exactly realized velocity residual (eq. 4) scaled by the noise level. This identity connects a mistake in the predicted sample to a correction in the velocity field. We first theoretically prove the relationship between the realized velocity residual and the clean prediction (section 3.1). In practice, the refiner is a transformer that predicts the velocity residual from three sources of information: i) the current answer, given by the one-step clean prediction, ii) the circumstances, given by the generation condition and noise level, and iii) the internal state, given by hidden states from the base model (Epstein et al., 2023). During joint training, clean samples and their sampled noise provide residual targets for the refiner, while the base model and refiner optimize separate objectives. During generation, the predicted residual adjusts the velocity used by the sampler before each state update. All refiner inputs reuse the same base-model forward pass, and each correction requires one additional refiner evaluation.

We empirically apply CorrFlow to a wide range of applications, including image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation. Figure 1 illustrates how this review shifts the model’s clean prediction through a correction of its velocity on image generation. We find that training a refiner improves the base model’s performance on aesthetic quality and physics consistency of generated content. The strong performance across multiple tasks and datasets shows that velocity residual correction is generic. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that learns velocity residuals from the base model’s current prediction, and applies the resulting corrections within the sampling loop.

  • •

    We theoretically establish conditions under which reusing base-model representations outperforms raw-input affine predictors, refiner training achieves greater residual-risk reduction than continued base-model training at matched compute, and deployed correction lowers velocity error under its own sampler-induced state law.

  • •

    We evaluate CorrFlow on image and video generation benchmarks, demonstrating improvements in visual quality and physics consistency.

2 Related Works

Improving Flow-Matching Generative Models. Many approaches have been proposed to improve flow-matching generative models. For representation learning, REPA (Yu et al., 2025) aligns hidden states with pretrained visual features, while iREPA (Singh et al., 2025) emphasizes their spatial structure. VA-VAE (Yao et al., 2025) aligns VAE latents with visual features, REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) jointly tunes the VAE and diffusion transformer through alignment and RAE (Zheng et al., 2026a) generates directly in pretrained representation spaces. Other methods reuse features available within the generative model: SRA and LayerSync (Jiang et al., 2026; Haghighi et al., 2026) use deeper features to guide shallower representations, and SRA2 (Wang et al., 2026a) draws on existing VAE features. Reward-based methods Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO (Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025c) use stochastic sampling for online reinforcement learning, while AWM (Xue et al., 2025b) and DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026c) incorporate rewards into flow-matching objectives through advantage weighting and paired generations, respectively. CorrFlow takes a complementary approach: it trains a lightweight added-on refiner to predict velocity residuals from the base model’s current prediction and hidden states. These residuals directly correct the velocity within the sampling loop, without requiring external representation teachers or reward models for refiner training.

Physics-Aware Video Generation. Several recent works have explored physics-aware video generation with flow-matching models. WISA (Wang et al., 2025), PhysVid (Pathak et al., 2026) and PhyParam (Li et al., 2026) inject hierarchical, temporally local, or instance-level physical conditions. PhysGen (Liu et al., 2024) and PSIVG (Foo et al., 2026) use simulated dynamics as guidance. Representation-based methods transfer or jointly learn motion, geometry, semantics and latent dynamics, including VideoREPA (Zhang et al., 2025c), PhysAlign (Xiong et al., 2026), VideoJAM (Chefer et al., 2025), PHANTOM (Shen et al., 2026), DreamWorld (Tan et al., 2026) and MMPhysVideo (Lin et al., 2026). Other approaches use language or feedback, with PhyT2V (Xue et al., 2025a) and DiffPhy (Zhang et al., 2025b) introducing inferred physical rules, PhysMaster (Ji et al., 2025) and PhyGDPO (Cai et al., 2025) applying pairwise or groupwise preference learning and WMReward (Yuan et al., 2026) steering denoising trajectories with a latent-world-model reward at inference. In contrast, CorrFlow learns to correct the base model’s own velocity residuals from its predictions and hidden states, without explicit physical parameters or external physics evaluators.

3 CorrFlow

CorrFlow augments a base flow-matching model 𝒇base\bm{f}_{\mathrm{base}} with a lightweight refiner that corrects its velocity 𝒗𝜽\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}} at each sampling step. We use bold upright symbols for samples, bold italic symbols for other vectors and tensors and ordinary symbols for scalars. The refiner takes the one-step clean prediction 𝐱^0=𝐱σ−σ​𝒗𝜽\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}=\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}-\sigma\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}, hidden states {𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}, conditioning 𝒄\bm{c} and noise-level embedding 𝒆σ\bm{e}_{\sigma} to predict a velocity residual:

𝒓^=𝒇refiner​(𝐱^0,{𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L,𝒄,𝒆σ),𝒗κ=𝒗𝜽+κ​𝒓^,\hat{\bm{r}}=\bm{f}_{\mathrm{refiner}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0},\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L},\bm{c},\bm{e}_{\sigma}),\qquad\bm{v}^{\kappa}=\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}+\kappa\hat{\bm{r}}, (1)

where κ\kappa controls the correction strength.

3.1 Preliminaries: flow matching and the residual it leaves behind

Let 𝐱0∈ℝD\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be the continuous representation of a clean data sample, with encoded conditioning 𝒄\bm{c}, such as class or text embeddings. The representation uses the sample’s native coordinates or a learned feature space, and DD denotes its dimension. Let 𝜺∼𝒩⁡(0,ID)\bm{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{D}) be independent noise in the same space. For a noise level σ∈[0,1]\sigma\in[0,1] the rectified-flow interpolant and its derivative are

𝐱σ=(1−σ)​𝐱0+σ​𝜺,d​𝐱σd​σ=𝜺−𝐱0.\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}=(1-\sigma)\,\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma\,\bm{\varepsilon},\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}}{\mathrm{d}\sigma}=\bm{\varepsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0}. (2)

The target flow velocity is 𝒗=𝜺−𝐱0\bm{v}=\bm{\varepsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0}, and the Bayes velocity field is 𝒗⋆(𝐱,σ,𝒄)=𝔼[𝜺−𝐱0∣𝐱σ=𝐱,𝒄]\bm{v}^{\star}(\mathbf{x},\sigma,\bm{c})=\mathbb{E}[\,\bm{\varepsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}=\mathbf{x},\bm{c}\,]. The base diffusion model 𝒇base\bm{f}_{\text{base}} is trained by

ℒbase​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐱0,𝒄,𝜺,σ​w​(σ)​∥𝒗𝜽​(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄)−𝒗∥2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\bm{c},\bm{\varepsilon},\sigma}\,w(\sigma)\,\big\lVert\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c})-\bm{v}\big\rVert^{2}, (3)

with w⁡(σ)w(\sigma) the noise-level weight of the base recipe, where 𝒗𝜽\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}} is the output of 𝒇base\bm{f}_{\text{base}}, parameterized by 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Generation integrates the learned velocity field d​𝐱/d​σ=𝒗𝜽​(𝐱,σ,𝒄)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}/\mathrm{d}\sigma=\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x},\sigma,\bm{c}) from σ=1\sigma=1 to σ=0\sigma=0 with explicit Euler steps on a shifted grid. The base model approximates the Bayes velocity field, while each sampled data–noise pair provides a realized target velocity. We call the difference between this target and the base prediction the realized velocity residual,

𝒓=𝒗−𝒗𝜽​(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄)=(𝜺−𝐱0)−𝒗𝜽​(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄).\bm{r}\;=\;\bm{v}-\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c})\;=\;(\bm{\varepsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0})-\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c}). (4)

This is the mistake we want the refiner 𝒇refiner\bm{f}_{\text{refiner}} to predict. The base model’s one-step clean prediction is available at generation time. Its discrepancy from the clean target is proportional to the realized velocity residual, as the following identity shows.

Clean-prediction identity.

Taking a single Euler step from 𝐱σ\mathbf{x}_{\sigma} all the way to σ=0\sigma=0 gives the base model’s one-step clean prediction, its best current guess at the finished sample,

𝐱^0​(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄)=𝐱σ−σ​𝒗𝜽​(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄).\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c})\;=\;\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}-\sigma\,\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c}). (5)

Substituting Equation 2 into Equation 5 and using Equation 4,

𝐱^0−𝐱0=σ⁡((𝜺−𝐱0)−𝒗𝜽)=σ​𝒓,equivalently𝒓=𝐱^0−𝐱0σ,σ>0.\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}-\mathbf{x}_{0}=\sigma\big((\bm{\varepsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0})-\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}\big)=\sigma\,\bm{r},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\bm{r}=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}-\mathbf{x}_{0}}{\sigma},\quad\sigma>0. (6)

This identity holds for any predictor 𝒗𝜽\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}} and shows that the clean-prediction error is the velocity residual 𝒓\bm{r} scaled by the noise level σ\sigma. It therefore motivates using 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} as the refiner’s primary input, expressing the prediction in the clean data space. Although 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} is available at every sampling step, its error depends on the unknown clean target. The refiner thus learns to estimate the residual from this prediction 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} and the accompanying features 𝒉L\bm{h}_{L}.

3.2 Refiner Inputs

Focusing on the current answer in isolation is insufficient, because the same prediction may be correct under one condition and a mistake under another, or an artifact that must be repaired at high noise may be a legitimate detail at low noise. Therefore, the refiner is given three views of the moment the mistake was made:

The current answer.

The one-step clean prediction 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} of Equation 5, tokenized according to the sample structure to form the refiner’s trunk tokens. This is the base model’s current estimate of the clean sample.

The circumstances.

The conditioning tokens 𝒄\bm{c} that encode the task requirements, and the noise level σ\sigma, which identifies the current position along the denoising trajectory.

The internal state.

The base model’s hidden states {𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}, where LL indexes transformer blocks selected uniformly across the model’s depth. These readouts capture different stages of the computation that produced 𝒗𝜽\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}, and they record how the prediction was assembled rather than only what it was.

Formally, let W=(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄)W=(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c}) denote the base model’s query state, and let 𝒵⁡(W)=(𝐱^0,{𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L,σ,𝒄)\mathcal{Z}(W)=(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0},\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L},\sigma,\bm{c}) be the refiner’s information. The refiner is a network 𝒇refiner\bm{f}_{\text{refiner}} with parameter vector ϕ\bm{\phi}, written as 𝒈ϕ\bm{g}_{\bm{\phi}}, and is trained to predict the residual, 𝒓^=𝒈ϕ​(𝒵⁡(W))≈𝒓.\hat{\bm{r}}\;=\;\bm{g}_{\bm{\phi}}(\mathcal{Z}(W))\;\approx\;\bm{r}. Every component of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is from the base model’s conditioning and its existing forward pass. Constructing them for the refiner requires no additional base-model evaluation and no access to the clean target at generation time.

3.3 Refiner architecture

CorrFlow is designed to be a lightweight add-on transformer to a base flow-matching model, which estimates the realized velocity residual 𝒓\bm{r}. It has its own parameters, totaling approximately 10%10\% of the base model’s parameter count. It carries the aforementioned information as inputs.

Token embeddings. Given the clean prediction 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} (eq. 5), the refiner 𝒇refiner\bm{f}_{\text{refiner}} first tokenizes it according to the sample structure into NN tokens and projects them to the refiner width dd, obtaining the answer tokens 𝒕ans∈ℝN×d\bm{t}_{\text{ans}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}. Our image and video implementations use patches for this tokenization. To keep the refiner and base model on a common clock, the refiner also consumes the base model’s own noise-level embedding 𝒆σ\bm{e}_{\sigma} at the current noise level σ\sigma.

We also construct the context tokens 𝒕ctx∈ℝ(Nc+N)×d\bm{t}_{\text{ctx}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N_{c}+N)\times d} from the conditioning 𝒄\bm{c} and the hidden states {𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}, where NcN_{c} is the number of conditioning tokens. In particular, a linear projection maps 𝒄\bm{c} to the conditioning tokens 𝒕c∈ℝNc×d\bm{t}_{\text{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{c}\times d}. At each token position, we concatenate the hidden states from the selected layers along the feature dimension and project them to the refiner width dd using a multilayer perceptron with a GELU activation,

𝒕fuse=MLP⁡(concatℓ∈L​𝒉ℓ)∈ℝN×d.\bm{t}_{\mathrm{fuse}}=\mathrm{MLP}\Bigl(\mathrm{concat}_{\ell\in L}\,\bm{h}_{\ell}\Bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}. (7)

This fusion across layers at fixed token positions is a deliberate choice. It keeps the hidden-state tokens at NN tokens instead of |L|⋅N|L|\cdot N, so attention cost does not grow with the number of readouts, and it lets the refiner learn which depth to trust at each location rather than committing to a fixed average across depths. To combine the two context tokens for the refiner’s cross-attention, we concatenate them along the token axis and apply layer normalization,

𝒕ctx=LayerNorm⁡([𝒕c+𝒔cond,𝒕fuse+𝒔state])∈ℝ(Nc+N)×d,\bm{t}_{\text{ctx}}=\mathrm{LayerNorm}\Bigl(\bigl[\,\bm{t}_{\text{c}}+\bm{s}_{\mathrm{cond}}\;,\;\bm{t}_{\text{fuse}}+\bm{s}_{\mathrm{state}}\,\bigr]\Bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{(N_{c}+N)\times d}, (8)

where 𝒔cond\bm{s}_{\mathrm{cond}} and 𝒔state\bm{s}_{\mathrm{state}} are learned segment embeddings that mark the two sources.

Alternating-Attention blocks. We build our lightweight add-on transformer with a stack of BB Alternating Attention Blocks (AABs), making the refiner focus on the current answer while consulting the context in an alternate manner. Specifically, even-indexed blocks apply self-attention to the answer tokens 𝒕ans\bm{t}_{\text{ans}}, using rotary position embeddings defined on the token coordinates of the sample representation. Our image and video implementations use two-dimensional spatial coordinates and three-dimensional spatiotemporal coordinates, respectively. Odd-indexed blocks apply cross-attention to the context tokens 𝒕ctx\bm{t}_{\text{ctx}}, which lets each token incorporate the task requirements and the base model’s intermediate representations. Each attention layer is followed by a feed-forward network. Following the base model’s adaptive-normalization design, each block uses shift, scale and gate parameters derived from the noise-level embedding 𝒆σ\bm{e}_{\sigma}. Finally, a modulated linear head projects the updated answer tokens to residual tokens, which are reassembled into the sample’s original shape.

3.4 Training and Inference

Objective.

We train the base model 𝒇base\bm{f}_{\text{base}} and the refiner 𝒇refiner\bm{f}_{\text{refiner}} on the same minibatch using separate objectives and a single backward pass. In particular, we define the refiner’s loss by a combination of a magnitude term and a direction term,

ℒref​(ϕ)=𝔼⁡[∥𝒓^−sg⁡[𝒓]∥2+λ⁡(1−cos⁡(𝒓^,sg⁡[𝒓]))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\bm{\phi})=\mathbb{E}\Big[\;\big\lVert\hat{\bm{r}}-\mathrm{sg}[\bm{r}]\big\rVert^{2}\;+\;\lambda\big(1-\cos\big(\hat{\bm{r}},\,\mathrm{sg}[\bm{r}]\big)\big)\Big], (9)

where sg⁡[⋅]\mathrm{sg}[\cdot] denotes the stop-gradient operator, 𝒓^=𝒇refiner​(sg⁡[𝒵⁡(W)])\hat{\bm{r}}=\bm{f}_{\text{refiner}}(\mathrm{sg}[\mathcal{Z}(W)]) is the refiner output, with 𝒓\bm{r} the realized velocity residual defined in Equation 4 and λ\lambda controls the weight of the direction term. We calculate the cosine similarity by flattening the overall residual field into a single vector per sample. The two terms play complementary roles. The squared-error term fits the residual vector, coupling its magnitude and direction. When residual directions vary across samples with similar refiner inputs, averaging these targets can produce a correction with a smaller magnitude. The cosine term explicitly rewards alignment with the target direction and complements this vector regression while the correction magnitude is learned. The total training objective is

ℒ=ℒbase​(𝜽)+λref​ℒref​(ϕ),\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}(\bm{\theta})+\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\bm{\phi}), (10)

where 𝜽\bm{\theta} and ϕ\bm{\phi} are the base and refiner parameters, respectively. Here λref\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} controls the relative weight of the refiner objective.

Inference.

The refiner is applied inside the ordinary sampling loop rather than as a post-process on a finished sample. At each denoising step the sampler evaluates the base model on the current sample, captures 𝒆σ\bm{e}_{\sigma} and {𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L} from that same evaluation, assembles 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} from Equation 5 and runs the refiner once on 𝒵⁡(W)\mathcal{Z}(W). The predicted residual is added to the base velocity with a gain κ\kappa,

𝒗κ=𝒗𝜽​(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄)+κ​𝒇refiner​(𝒵⁡(W)),\bm{v}^{\kappa}=\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c})+\kappa\,\bm{f}_{\text{refiner}}(\mathcal{Z}(W)), (11)

and the corrected velocity is what the scheduler integrates. Because 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} and {𝒉ℓ}ℓ∈L\{\bm{h}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L} are obtained from the state the sampler has actually reached, each correction influences subsequent refiner inputs. This adds one refiner forward pass per step without additional base-model evaluations.

4 Theoretical Analysis

We analyze three complementary questions: whether frozen base-model features can improve residual prediction beyond raw-input predictors, whether refiner training can outperform continued base-model training at matched budget and whether a trained correction improves velocity error under the state law it induces at deployment.

Shared residual target. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a finite-dimensional Hilbert sample space, let PP be the law of the query state W=(𝐱σ,σ,𝒄)W=(\mathbf{x}_{\sigma},\sigma,\bm{c}) and let P~\widetilde{P} be the joint law of (W,𝒓)(W,\bm{r}) at the fixed base checkpoint used below. 5 Experiments

We evaluate CorrFlow on a wide range of tasks, including class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation. The image experiments test whether learned velocity corrections improve an established flow-matching model, while the video experiments examine visual quality, temporal consistency and physical plausibility. Red, orange and yellow highlight the best, second-best and third-best scores in each column, respectively.

5.1 Image Generation

Settings. We study class-conditional generation on ImageNet at 256×256256\times 256 resolution with 1,000 classes. Our base model is built upon RAEv2 with a frozen DINOv3-L-based representation autoencoder and a pretrained diffusion transformer. Starting from its 80-epoch checkpoint, we jointly fine-tune the base transformer and train a randomly initialized refiner for another 80 epochs on the ImageNet training split, denoted by 80+8080+80 in Table 1. The refiner has 10 transformer blocks with width 768 and 12 attention heads, and reads hidden states from base transformer blocks 3, 11, 19 and 27, using one-based indexing. We retain the base model’s training objective and train the refiner to predict the realized velocity residual with squared error and a cosine-direction term weighted by 0.10.1. Both networks use GMuon optimizer with a global batch size of 1,024. The evaluation settings are identical to those in Singh et al. (2026).

Results. Table 1 compares CorrFlow with RAEv2 at a matched budget of 160 total epochs, because our 80+8080+80 schedule spends 80 epochs on the base checkpoint and 80 epochs on joint training. Under this budget, CorrFlow improves over RAEv2 on IS and on all three FDr\mathrm{FD}_{r} metrics, both with and without guidance, so the gain comes from the learned residual corrections rather than from a longer training schedule. With guidance, CorrFlow leads on every metric in the table, surpassing SiT-XL/2 and RAE-XL trained for 800 epochs. It also outperforms the evaluated SelfFlow variant in both guidance settings. Additional results are provided in Section E.1.

5.2 Text-to-Video Generation

Settings. We use Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (Wan et al., 2025) as the base model and jointly adapt its transformer with the refiner on video–text pairs from WISA-80K (Wang et al., 2025) and OpenVidHD (Nan et al., 2025). The refiner has 10 transformer blocks with width 1,024 and 16 attention heads, and reads hidden states from base blocks 4, 12, 20 and 30, using one-based indexing. The final training stage uses 66,572 clips for five epochs with AdamW and a global batch size of 16, retaining the base flow-matching objective and a residual objective with cosine-direction weight 0.10.1. We generate 81-frame videos at 480×832480\times 832 resolution with 50 Euler steps and evaluate visual quality and temporal consistency with VBench (Huang et al., 2024), and physical plausibility and prompt adherence with VideoPhy2 (Bansal et al., 2026) and FinePhyEval (Pothiraj et al., 2026). Section D.2 provides the training and evaluation details.

Results. Table 2 reports the VideoPhy2 and FinePhyEval results for physics-consistent text-to-video generation. CorrFlow achieves the highest VideoPhy2 Joint scores on both ALL and HARD, increasing them from 24.824.8 to 27.027.0 and from 5.65.6 to 6.96.9, respectively, over Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. It also achieves the highest FinePhyEval Overall score of 0.600.60, with improvements in object, action and physics scores over the same base model. On VBench (table 3), CorrFlow leads the compared methods on Quality Score and Overall Score, reaching 84.6984.69 and 81.8681.86. Figure 3 shows the same advantage in the generated frames, where CorrFlow carries each prompted interaction to its physical outcome, dropping the domino into the mug and landing the coin in the metal cup, while the baselines lose the object or drift away from the prompted action. These results show that the adapted model improves both general video quality and the joint satisfaction of semantic and physical requirements. Section E.2 analyzes the full metric breakdown.

5.3 Image-to-Video Generation

Settings. We use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan et al., 2025) as the base model, with the same training data, objectives, optimization and five-epoch schedule as in Section 5.2. We enable first-frame image conditioning for 40%40\% of training examples and use text-only conditioning for the remainder. The refiner has 13 transformer blocks with width 2,048 and 32 attention heads, reading hidden states from the same base blocks as in text-to-video generation. We evaluate on the 198 image–text pairs of Physics-IQ Verified (Rädsch et al., 2026; Motamed et al., 2026), generating 81-frame videos at 704×1248704\times 1248 resolution with the same sampling configuration as in text-to-video generation. Section D.3 details the image conditioning, training and evaluation.

Results. Table 4 reports the Physics-IQ Verified results. CorrFlow achieves the highest Verified Score of 30.9530.95, and leads on Spatial, Weighted Spatial and MSE Score. These results indicate closer agreement with the ground-truth videos in motion coverage and frame appearance. Figure 4 illustrates shadow and object consistency, with the statuette’s shadow tracking the moving light and the blade separating the mandarin into halves. Section E.3 provides the metric breakdown and qualitative analysis.

5.4 Ablation Study

We conduct a number of ablations to nanalyze the contribution of each component. All variants are built on WAN-2.1-T2V-1.3B (Wan et al., 2025) and follow the same training protocol. Specifically, each model is trained for five epochs on the same 1,000 samples from WISA-80K (Wang et al., 2025). We evaluate on a disjoint set of 50 WISA-80K samples selected to provide approximately uniform coverage over the physical categories. We report visual quality and consistency metrics from VBench, together with its aggregate Quality Score. Results are reported in Table 5.

The full model achieves the highest Quality Score and leads on all visual quality and consistency metrics. Removing cross-attention causes the largest score drop, closely followed by self-attention, highlighting the value of context and spatiotemporal interactions in the base model’s prediction. Removing either the refiner or hidden-state MLP reduces Quality Score and Overall Consistency, supporting refinement and fusion of hidden states across depths. The remaining ablations produce smaller but consistent score decreases. Removing noise-level conditioning or replacing the clean prediction 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} with the velocity prediction 𝒗𝜽\bm{v}_{\bm{\theta}} lowers aggregate performance, supporting the value of noise-level information and explicit clean-sample estimates. Removing text conditioning lowers Quality Score and notably weakens Overall Consistency, suggesting its role in semantic alignment.

6 Conclusion

We introduced CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that learns velocity residuals from the base model’s clean prediction, conditioning and hidden states. A lightweight refiner corrects the velocity within the sampling loop. Our theory identifies conditions under which feature reuse improves residual prediction, refiner training outperforms continued base-model training at matched compute, and the deployed correction lowers own-law velocity error. We demonstrate that CorrFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks including image generation, text-to-video generation, and image-to-video generation. We hope CorrFlow will be a useful tool for the community to advance research in flow-matching-based generative modeling.
